KlisterFixer

We are redesigning how cross-country skiers apply klister wax. Our goal is to make the process cleaner, faster, and more consistent for all conditions.

Scroll

Our Mission

Engineering
for real
people.

As part of GEEN 2400: Engineering for the Community, our team is working on a client-based design project focused on health, safety, and quality of life. We are using the engineering design process to tackle a real problem that our client brought to us.

We are working directly with the CU Boulder Nordic Ski Club to improve how skiers apply klister wax to their skis. We have been meeting regularly with our client and are building a product that is practical, easy to use, and actually solves the problems they face out on the trail.

What We're Solving

Three Focus
Areas

Client Partnership

We are working directly with the CU Boulder Nordic Ski Club, founded in 2023. Getting to know them and understanding their real needs has been a big part of our process so far.

Problem Identification

Klister wax application is messy, inconsistent, and takes way too long. We talked with club members and identified the specific issues that make this process so frustrating in cold outdoor conditions.

Our Solutions

Our prototypes focus on cleanliness, temperature control, and ease of use. We want any skier, regardless of experience, to be able to wax their skis quickly and confidently before heading out.

The Capability Gap

One of the most important parts of Nordic skiing is prepping your skis before you head out. Klister wax needs to be applied to the base of the ski to give you the grip you need in icy or slushy conditions. The problem is that applying it is a messy, time-consuming process that is hard to do consistently. That is why the Nordic Ski Club came to us. They wanted help building something that makes this easier for all their members.

02

Root Issues

The
Problems

Why klister wax needs a better solution

Problem Statement

What Makes
Klister Difficult?

Klister is a tacky wax that goes on the bottom of cross-country skis to help with grip in icy, wet, or slushy conditions where regular hard wax does not work. To apply it, you have to heat the wax first and then spread thin layers onto the middle section of the ski called the kick zone. Getting it right makes a big difference in how the ski performs.

Our team is working on a new product to fix the issues with how klister is currently applied. After talking with the Nordic Ski Club, we identified the core problem: klister wax is hard to apply correctly because you need precise temperature control, even spreading, and a full cleanup afterward. The whole thing is slow, inconsistent, and really inconvenient when you are standing outside in the cold.

01

Cleanliness

Klister is extremely sticky and gets all over your hands, clothes, ski bags, and gear. Once it gets on something, it is almost impossible to remove without a solvent. This is probably the biggest complaint we heard from club members.

02

Temperature Control

Klister has to be at just the right temperature before it spreads properly. If it is too cold it will not move. If it gets too hot it drips everywhere. Trying to get that right while standing outside in winter is really difficult.

03

Time Consumption

The current process takes anywhere from 15 to 30 minutes. You have to heat the wax, spread it in layers, wait for it to set, and then clean everything up. That is a lot of time to spend in a cold parking lot before a ski outing.

04

Inconsistent Results

Without a good tool, it is hard to get even coverage every time. If the wax is uneven, your skis will not perform as well and you end up having to scrape it off and start over, which wastes both time and wax.

05

Outdoor Inconvenience

Most people apply klister at trailheads or in parking lots. If you wear gloves you cannot spread the wax properly, but if you take them off your hands get covered in klister. None of the current tools are designed with outdoor use in mind.

06

Portability

Klister tubes can leak in ski bags and contaminate everything inside. There is no good way to carry everything you need in one contained unit that will not make a mess on the way to the trailhead.

How Klister Is Applied Right Now

Looking at the current process step by step makes it clear why skiers find it so frustrating. Our goal is to simplify as many of these steps as we can.

01

Warm the klister tube with body heat or a small torch until pliable

02

Squeeze thin beads of wax onto the kick zone of the ski base

03

Spread evenly with a scraper or finger (major contamination risk)

04

Allow to partially set before skiing

05

Clean all tools, hands, and any contaminated surfaces after use

Solutions

Our Design Approach

How We
Designed It

After identifying the core problems with klister application, our team developed the KlisterFixer — a handheld, gun-style applicator designed to eliminate mess, deliver consistent temperature, and squeeze wax precisely onto the ski without any hand contact. Our design evolved significantly through client feedback and iterative prototyping.

Initial Concept Sketch — PDR

Concept Development

From Sketch to System

Our initial sketch established the core geometry: a rectangular housing body (5.5″ × 2.5″) paired with a pistol-grip handle at a downward angle. This layout keeps the device balanced and ergonomic while leaving room internally for the klister tube, heating element, and trigger mechanism.

The design moved away from our original open-tube concept after client feedback made it clear that any exposed wax surface would create the same contamination problems we were trying to solve.

Ergonomic Housing

The 3D-printed housing fully encloses the klister tube and loads from the side, so the wax never touches the user's hands. A round handle — informed directly by ski team feedback — improves grip in gloved hands and distributes weight toward the back of the device.

Trigger Squeeze Mechanism

Inspired by a hot glue gun, a funnel-shaped compression system wraps around the klister tube and squeezes inward when the trigger is pulled. This delivers consistent, controlled pressure without the user needing to touch the wax or tube directly.

Thermal Control Circuit

A resistive heating element warms the klister to its working temperature. An Arduino reads a thermistor and controls two LEDs — one for power-on, one for ready-temperature — so the user always knows when the wax is ready to apply without any guesswork.

Prototype 01

Circuit
Design

Circuit Idea

From Simple Resistance to Smart Sensing

Our original idea for the circuit was simply to connect the heating element (resistor) to the battery. We thought this idea would be great for its simplicity and effectiveness.

After talking to Annika from the CU Ski Team, we decided to add two LEDs — one to show when the Klister Gun is on, and another to show when the machine has reached operating temperature. To ensure we can read the temperature, we will also use a thermistor to control the LEDs.

Prototype 02

Trigger
Compression System

Concept A

Hot Glue Gun Inspired Applicator

Our prototype is inspired by the trigger mechanism of a hot glue gun but adapted specifically for a Klister ski wax bottle. Instead of advancing a solid stick, the trigger activates a funnel-shaped compression system that wraps around the bottle and squeezes inward.

The funnel pivots from the front, causing greater compression at the rear of the bottle and gradually less toward the front, which creates a controlled and directed flow of liquid wax through the nozzle.

This design improves pressure distribution, reduces material waste, and allows for smoother, more consistent wax application while keeping the mechanism simple and ergonomic.

Physical Prototype

Sizing & Squeeze Mechanism Validation

This prototype was built to test the sizing for the Klister Gun. We wanted to make sure we could create a housing that would fit the klister tube and validate the 'squeeze' mechanism. We also needed to confirm that the overall size was appropriate for a handheld device.

Additionally, we included a pivot point to test various trigger mechanisms in subsequent iterations.

Client Feedback — CU Ski Team

Team Response & Iteration Notes

The ski team loved this prototype. They thought the size was great and that the device would be genuinely beneficial. Key feedback included:

  • → The square handle is difficult to grip — a round handle would be preferable.
  • → More weight should be distributed to the handle so the device isn't top-heavy.
  • → Side-loading wax was appreciated — it allows cleaning of the inside container.
  • → A cover for the front applicator would be helpful to protect against klister buildup during storage.
